text: An oracle concerning the wilderness by the sea: Like storm winds sweeping through the Negev, it comes from the desert, from a land of terror.
A harsh vision has been told to me: the traitor betrays, the destroyer destroys. Go up, Elam! Lay siege, Media! I have put an end to all her groaning.

versions.text: A harsh vision has been shown to me: the traitor betrays, the destroyer destroys. Go up, Elam! Lay siege, Media! I have put an end to all her groaning.
versions.explanation: הֻגַּד is from נגד, 'to declare, tell, report' (the same root used in verses 6 and 10, both rendered 'report/declared'). 'Shown' shifts the image from announcement to sight and breaks the chapter's consistent vocabulary.

text: Therefore my body is racked with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor. I am doubled over by what I hear; I am terrified by what I see.
My heart staggers, horror overwhelms me; the twilight I longed for has become my dread.
Set the table! Post the lookout! Eat, drink! Get up, you officers! Oil the shields!

versions.text: They set the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink—"Get up, you officers! Oil the shields!"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew forms are infinitives absolute used as commands (Set the table, watch the watch/post the lookout, eat, drink), not narrative past. Also צָפֹה הַצָּפִית more likely refers to posting a lookout, which fits the watchman theme of the chapter, rather than spreading rugs.

versions.text: Set the table! Post the lookout! Eat, drink!—"Get up, you officers! Oil the shields!"
versions.explanation: The verse now has an unmatched closing quotation mark: a quoted phrase appears without any introduction of a speaker, and the surrounding commands are unquoted. Since all four clauses are commands in the same voice, dropping the quotation marks (and the dash) makes the line consistent and easier to read aloud.

text: For this is what the Lord said to me: "Go, post a watchman, and let him report what he sees.
When he sees a chariot with a pair of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen closely, very closely."

versions.text: When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen closely, very closely."
versions.explanation: רֶכֶב here denotes a chariot/mounted troop; rendering it 'riders' and then repeating 'riders on donkeys' loses the parallel structure of רֶכֶב חֲמוֹר / רֶכֶב גָּמָל. Suggest 'chariot' for the first item.

text: Then the lookout called out like a lion: "On the watchtower, my Lord, I stand all day long, and at my post I keep guard through every night.

versions.text: Then the watchman called out: "On the watchtower, my Lord, I stand all day long, and at my post I keep guard through every night.
versions.explanation: The word אַרְיֵה ('a lion') is omitted; the Hebrew says he cried out like a lion (i.e., with a roar). The current rendering drops content present in the text.

text: Look—here comes a chariot of men, a pair of horsemen!" And he answered and said: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground."

versions.text: Look—here comes a column of riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered and said: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground."
versions.explanation: Verse 7 was deliberately revised to render רֶכֶב as 'chariot,' but the same phrase here (רֶכֶב ... צֶמֶד פָּרָשִׁים) is rendered 'column of riders,' losing the intentional link between the watchman's instructions and his report. 'Column' is also not in the Hebrew.

text: O my threshed people, my child of the threshing floor, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you.

versions.text: My people, threshed and winnowed on the floor, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you.
versions.explanation: 'Winnowed' is not in the Hebrew; בֶּן־גָּרְנִי is 'son/child of my threshing floor.' A closer rendering preserves the imagery without adding a term.

text: An oracle concerning Dumah: Someone calls to me from Seir, "Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?"
The watchman answers, "Morning is coming, and night as well. If you must inquire, then inquire; come back again."

versions.text: The watchman answers, "Morning is coming, but also the night. If you must ask, come back and ask again."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two imperatives, 'ask/inquire' then 'return, come'; the current rendering reverses the order and blurs the sense. Also 'but also the night' reads more smoothly as 'and night as well.'

text: An oracle concerning Arabia: In the thickets of Arabia you must camp for the night, you caravans of Dedan.
Bring water to the thirsty, you who live in the land of Tema; meet the fugitive with bread.
For they flee from the swords—from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, from the weight of battle.

versions.text: For they flee from the swords—from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, from the fury of battle.
versions.explanation: כֹּבֶד means 'heaviness/weight, pressure'; 'fury' shifts the image. 'Weight of battle' keeps the Hebrew metaphor and reads well aloud.

text: For this is what the Lord said to me: "Within one year, as a hired worker counts the years, all the splendor of Kedar will come to an end.
And the remnant of the bowmen, the warriors of the sons of Kedar, will be few." For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.

versions.text: And the survivors of the archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few." For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.
versions.explanation: בְנֵי־קֵדָר ('the sons of Kedar') is flattened to 'Kedar'; also מִסְפַּר־קֶשֶׁת conveys 'the number of the bows,' so 'remnant of the bowmen' is closer than 'survivors of the archers.'
